name: P1-intro
question: Thanks for taking the time. Could you introduce yourself and pick one Android project you worked on? Who used it and which part did you personally own?
candidate: I worked on Android and AI travel planning at KKday. The product helps travelers put together an itinerary using their destination, budget and trip length. I can explain the Android side in more detail.

card.problem: Introduce yourself and pick one Android project: who used it and which part you personally owned
card.heard: introduce yourself and pick one Android project
card.say: Good evening, I'm Jianhui. I have ten years of experience in software development, mainly working on Android apps. Over the past three years, I've also been working on AI products, from development to launch. My most recent job was at KKday, a travel platform in Asia. I worked on the main features of the Android app and made the app run faster. For example, I fixed the lag when users switched between product options. At the same time, I was the technical lead for an AI trip planning project. I was responsible for the technical plan, the agent architecture, and the main backend development. After we launched it, the system handled about 300,000 trip planning requests every day. Before KKday, I worked at Kezhi Technology, an AI education startup. I was the only Android engineer there. I built the Android app and worked with my team to launch the first version in just four weeks. That's also when I started working on AI features myself. Before that, I worked on Android apps at Debon Securities.

name: W2-design
question: Users are signed in. This is a centralized single-currency USD wallet with internal transfers, no fees, and a server-owned ledger. Include balance, transfer, history and details. Cache reads can work offline, but submissions require a network. A has 100 dollars and B starts at zero. Draw the flow for A to send B 80 dollars, from confirmation through the result, including Android and the service.
candidate: For the first design I expect a synchronous internal transfer. A confirms in the app, the Android client submits one request, and the server updates both ledger balances atomically. I show the result from the service in that same request and keep a local read cache. I am assuming there is no async outcome recovery screen in this design.

card.heard: what should the server do if the same requestId arrives with a different amount
card.say: The server should reject it. A requestId belongs to one transfer, so the amount is part of that record. If the amount doesn't match, the server returns a conflict error and changes nothing. candidate: Each transfer has a distinct intent ID. The server serializes or conditionally updates the available balance within the transaction. One transfer commits, the other is rejected for insufficient funds, and the clients refresh their balance.

card.problem: Introduce yourself and pick one Android project: who used it and which part you personally owned
card.constraints: ["A logs out while a request is in flight and C signs in before the response arrives; the app must not show or store A\'s result under C"]
card.heard: A logs out mid-request, C signs in before the response
card.say: The risk is that A's response lands after C is signed in. If the app just shows whatever comes back, C could see A's transfer result, or A's pending state could be saved under C's account. So I'd tie every request and every saved intent to the user who started it. When the response arrives, the app checks the current session against that owner. If they don't match, it drops the UI update and only writes the result into A's own stored data.

There are two contacts called Alex and no reliable amount in the messages. Revise the entry flow. After the user confirms, the chat can disconnect.
candidate: I would ask the user to choose the correct Alex and provide the amount, open a trustworthy native wallet confirmation, and require authorization for the displayed transaction. The payment has its own status and can be recovered in wallet history when the chat disconnects.

card.heard: agent tool called twice, second call has a different amount after confirmation
card.say: Only the first call can be accepted. The amount the user saw and approved is the one that counts. So the service should accept the call that matches the confirmed amount and the saved intent ID. The second call with a different amount must be rejected, because the user never approved it. If the agent really needs a new amount, it has to go back to the user for a fresh confirmation.

card.say: I'd ship the core loop first: balance, send, history and details, with the intent ID and the pending state. That's the smallest thing users can trust. To verify it, I'd test the lost-response case and the logout case, then roll out to a small group and watch the pending count. If pending transfers spike in the first half hour, I'd first check whether the service is slow or the responses are being lost. I'd keep the app in the pending state, not show a failure, and let users retry with the same intent ID.
